Short-term yields: annualising a discount does not create a year of cash income

Separate a discount security’s holding-period gain from three explicit annualisation formulas, then compare the same starting cash at the same end date.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore holding-period profit and explicitly defined annualisations

Interactive planning lab

Cash gain during the selected holding period$110
Return over the selected holding period1.11%
Effective annualised mathematical equivalent2.27%

Hypothetical discount security held to a known maturity payment, with purchase price between 90% and 100% of that amount. No fees, tax, default, early sale or actual quote. All annualisations deliberately use 365 days. Price-based simple annualisation divides profit by purchase price; face-based annualisation divides by maturity amount. The effective annualised equivalent compounds the holding-period factor to a year and does not establish an available reinvestment rate. The comparison account uses the same initial cash and selected holding days at an assumed effective annual rate.

The central idea

The dollar gain occurs over the actual holding days. An annualised equivalent changes the time basis of a calculation; it does not guarantee repeated investments or another year of cash payments.

01

Start with the two cash amounts and the days between them

A short-term discount security can be purchased for less than the amount paid at maturity. The difference is a gain over the holding period. A quoted annual rate can help compare calculations, but it should not replace the actual dollars and dates in a cash plan.

The AMF’s debt-securities overview describes Treasury-bill return as the difference between purchase price and the amount received at maturity. This article creates its own hypothetical discount example and does not reproduce a current auction, dealer quote or security recommendation.

The default maturity payment is CAD 10,000. The purchase price is 98.9% of that amount, or CAD 9,890, and maturity is 180 days later. No fee or tax is included. The gain during those 180 days is therefore CAD 110. The waterfall reconciles the initial amount invested with the maturity receipt.

02

Calculate the return on the money actually invested

The holding-period return divides the CAD 110 gain by the CAD 9,890 purchase price. The result is approximately 1.1122% over 180 days. That is the return on the starting investment under the selected terms.

Dividing the gain by the CAD 10,000 maturity amount instead produces 1.10%. That calculation uses a different denominator. It is a discount relative to the maturity payment, rather than the return on cash paid at purchase.

The two percentages are close in this example, but their meanings are different. A larger discount makes the denominator distinction more visible. The model limits purchase price to 90% through 100% of the maturity amount so that it studies discount and zero-discount cases; it does not model purchasing a security above its maturity amount.

03

Read each annualisation formula before comparing its number

The first annualised measure multiplies the purchase-price-based holding return by 365 ÷ 180. Under the defaults, this simple annualisation is approximately 2.2554%. The face-based measure uses the maturity amount in the denominator and is approximately 2.2306%.

The effective annualised equivalent uses the factor (10,000 ÷ 9,890)365/180 − 1, giving approximately 2.2683%. It compounds the holding-period factor across a year, rather than multiplying the period return by the number of periods.

All three formulas in these charts deliberately use a 365-day year. Their labels define the conventions used here. The calculator does not assert that a particular market, dealer or instrument quotes yield this way. Confirm an actual quote’s price basis, day-count convention, settlement date and yield definition before comparing it with another product.

04

Compare the same starting money at the same final date

The comparison account starts with the same CAD 9,890 and earns an independently assumed 3% effective annual return for 180 days. Its endpoint is CAD 9,890 × 1.03180/365, or approximately CAD 10,035.22.

The discount security’s modeled maturity receipt is CAD 10,000. Under those assumptions, the account endpoint is about CAD 35.22 higher. The comparison uses the same starting cash and holding days, so it does not accidentally compare one full year of account growth with a shorter security term.

Both amounts are before fees and taxes, with no actual provider terms verified. The chart evaluates an amount calculation rather than safety, access, insurance coverage or suitability. A higher numerical endpoint under an assumed account rate does not establish that such a rate is available or that the two arrangements have the same risks.

05

Treat large short-period annualisations as a conditional equivalence

The matrix changes the price discount and holding days. Each cell annualises the resulting holding-period factor over a 365-day year. It does not assign a likelihood to any discount or claim that short-term opportunities can be repeated on the same terms.

For the same maturity amount and price discount, the dollar gain remains the same when the holding period changes. Receiving that gain sooner changes its annualised rate. It does not create a larger cash gain on that one purchase, and the annualised number should not be entered as additional money arriving at maturity.

When holding days equal 365, the effective annualised return and the purchase-price-based holding return coincide. At a zero discount, the modeled gain and every annualisation are zero. These boundary cases help distinguish a change in the time basis from a change in the actual cash amounts.

06

Bring costs and the maturity date back into the funding plan

A real purchase requires the executable price, quantity, settlement date, maturity date and any charges. Even a modest flat charge can materially reduce a small short-term dollar gain. Add those costs before relying on a return calculated from price and maturity alone.

The model assumes holding to the stated maturity payment. It does not forecast a sale price before maturity, model a missed payment or calculate a reinvestment strategy after the first term. An annualised equivalent is not evidence that another security will be available at the same price relationship when the money returns.

For planning, record how much cash leaves now and how much is expected on the actual maturity date under supported terms. Use a consistent return definition for comparisons, then keep the dollar funding calendar beside it. That preserves the distinction between a mathematical annual rate and the cash available to pay a particular bill.
